extracted.intended_audience: general readers and readers interested in 19th-century maritime fiction and practical seafaring advice
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a 19th-century sea-narrative (Poe's Arthur Gordon Pym) combining fictional narration of a mutiny and embedded practical guidance on ship stowage and handling. Useful both as literary source material and as historical maritime practice description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent cargo or ballast shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: The great point is to allow no possibility of the cargo or ballast shifting position even in the most violent rollings of the vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that stowage must be done so nothing can move during violent motion; pay attention to the bulk taken in and the nature of the bulk (full or partial cargo). Neglect in stowage is cited as the cause of many accidents and founderings; coasting vessels and hurried loading/discharging are especially liable. Example consequence: in a heavy lurch loose cargo can tumble to one side, prevent the vessel from righting, and cause sinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'screwing' for full loads of certain commodities
rubrics_metrics.description: In most kinds of freight the stowage is accomplished by means of a screw. Thus, in a load of tobacco or flour, the whole is screwed so tightly into the hold of the vessel that the barrels or hogsheads, upon discharging, are found to be completely flattened...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screwing packs cargo tightly to save room and prevents shifting in a full load (so long as cargo remains full). Warning: screwing can introduce other risks—certain cargoes (cotton, tobacco) may expand (e.g., through fermentation) and, when tightly screwed, can exert enough force to 'rend a vessel asunder.' Use screwing judiciously and consider the physical/chemical properties of the cargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stowage precautions for partial cargoes: shifting-boards and stanchions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a partial cargo is received... the whole, after being first stowed as compactly as may be, should be covered with a layer of stout shifting-boards, extending completely across the vessel. Upon these boards strong temporary stanchions should be erected, reaching to the timbers above, and thus securing every thing in its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For partial loads, take active measures to prevent shifting: use stout shifting-boards spanning the hold and erect strong temporary stanchions up to the timbers above. These precautions are essential because partial cargoes are most susceptible to movement in heavy rolls and can quickly cause catastrophic loss if they shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special precautions for grain and similar cargoes (settling and swelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cargoes consisting of grain, or any similar matter, additional precautions are requisite. A hold filled entirely with grain upon leaving port will be found not more than three fourths full upon reaching its destination... This result is occasioned by settling during the voyage... To prevent these, every method should be employed before leaving port to settle the cargo as much as possible; and for this there are many contrivances, among which may be mentioned the driving of wedges into the grain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grain settles and swells during passage, increasing shifting risk even when initially well secured. Before leaving port, apply methods to settle and compact the grain (e.g., driving wedges) and securely fasten shifting-boards and stanchions. Even with precautions, experienced seamen treat grain voyages with caution—partial grain cargoes remain particularly hazardous in heavy weather.
